May (just) As Well/Might (just) As Well
You use may as well and might as well to make suggestions. You use these phrases to suggest what you think is the easiest or most logical choice in a situation.

You use may as well when the situation you are talking about is fairly certain.
Example: I am off for the day. I may as well do all my Christmas shopping today. = I am certain to be off today. I can do my Christmas shopping.

You use might as well to suggest a higher level of uncertainty.
Example: I'm not sure when I'll get another break, so I might as well do my Christmas shopping today. = I'm not sure whether I'll have a break at another point in time, so I should do my Christmas shopping.
You might as well harness the power of the bright minds you employ.
You may as well sit down with your team on a regular basis and brainstorm ideas.
You might as well share that with the team and give them a pat on the back to show the team the value of their efforts and your appreciation.
You may just as well find that people want to be a part of that and will be motivated by it.
Note: The phrase just as well means a good or fortunate thing.
Using Should, Ought to, and Had Better
You use modals like should, ought to or had better to give advice.
The most common modals for giving advice are: should, ought to and had better.
You can think of modals as “helping verbs”. They add meaning to the main verb of a sentence. In this case, these modals add the meaning of advice.

Should is the most common modal used to give advice. You also use should for questions.
Ought to is used for giving strong advice.
Had better is much stronger than either should or ought to. It is used to give an order or to suggest that something negative will happen if you refuse the advice.

images.text:
Many restaurateurs are going green, but employee motivation may not be the first thing that comes to mind. Incorporating green practices into your restaurant has many employee-related benefits.
How can you increase employee motivation? It's simple. You might as well harness the power of the bright minds of your employees. You should ask your staff what they would like to see. How do they envision their ideal workplace? What is your organization not doing that would make a difference to your employees? You may as well sit down with your team on a regular basis and brainstorm ideas.

From there, you ought to arm your employees with the power to use their skills and ideas to implement change that will benefit the organization. You'd better increase employee motivation further by offering incentives to the person that comes up with the most innovative idea to solve a problem, save energy, reduce water use or waste. By involving your employees in this process, the restaurant will benefit from a staff that is more engaged, proud and committed.

Keep the motivation going. You'd better share your successes and celebrate your accomplishments by rewarding your hard-working staff on a job well done. If your energy bills were down five per cent because of an employee's idea, you might as well share that with the team and give them a pat on the back to show the team the value of their efforts and your appreciation. When your organization is doing important things, you might just as well find that people want to be apart of that and will be motivated by it.
Creating a workplace that cares about the environment generates a feeling of pride among your employees which will result in a team that is excited about coming to work and making a difference in their community!
